**Project:** Madison Country Club Addition, 445 Country Club Rd, Madison FL 32340
**Job:** HDGA 2515 | **Sealed:** 2026-02-16 through 2026-02-18 | **43 Sheets**

---

> **Scope Clarification for the Reader:** This 43-sheet set is a **building-only construction document** for the clubhouse addition at Madison Golf and RV Resort. It is **not** a civil site-development plan set for an RV park or manufactured housing community (MHC). The horizontal infrastructure (RV site grids, roads, utilities to lots) is contained in a **separate 21-sheet civil set by Menadier Engineering** — that set was reviewed separately and is referenced here only where the two projects intersect. Accordingly, many of the standard MHP/RV civil plan-facts fields (site counts, road network, stormwater pond sizing, RV pedestal schedules, etc.) cannot be answered from this set. All such fields are marked UNKNOWN with an explanation.

# Madison Country Club Addition — AACE Class 4 Preliminary Cost Estimate
## Senior Civil/Construction Estimator and Project Manager Review

---

> **Critical framing note before any number is read:** This estimate covers **only the clubhouse addition building project** (HDGA 2515, 43-sheet set). It does NOT estimate the 215-site RV park expansion (Menadier Engineering set — a separate project). The "developed sites" metric at the end is therefore not meaningful in the traditional MHP/RV park $/site sense; I will explain this explicitly in that section and flag it rather than produce a misleading per-site number. The estimate is AACE Class 4 (−30% / +50% accuracy range), based on schematic/design-development level documents with the specific gaps and errors identified in the Plan Facts and Error Register stages.

---

## Regional Baseline and Labor/Material Multiplier

**Location:** Madison, FL 32340 (Madison County, Florida — rural North Florida, approximately 90 miles east of Tallahassee)

# Madison Country Club Addition — Value-Add & Value-Engineering Analysis
## Section 5: Alternatives Analysis
**Base Case Reference:** 43-sheet building construction document set, HDGA 2515, sealed 2026-02-16 through 2026-02-18

---

> **Critical framing note for the reader:** This 43-sheet set is a **building-only construction document** for the ~3,150–3,650 sf clubhouse addition at Madison Golf and RV Resort. It is **not** a civil site-development plan set for an RV park or manufactured housing community. The horizontal infrastructure (RV site grids, roads, stormwater, utility mains to lots) is in the separate Menadier Engineering set reviewed independently. Accordingly, many standard MHP/RV VE categories (road section, site pad type, lift station elimination, pedestal spec) apply to the **Menadier civil project**, not to this building set. Where a VE category does not apply to this building scope, I say so explicitly and redirect to where it does apply. Where it applies to both, I address both. **All NOI deltas are directional estimates based on 2025 golf/RV resort market knowledge and the Golf Life Navigators market data cited in the project brief; treat them as planning-level guidance, not an appraisal or feasibility study.**

---

## Base Case Cost Summary (Reconstructed from Plan Facts and Error Register)

| Cost Category | Base Case Estimate | Confidence | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Building construction (hard cost, as-designed) | $850,000–$1,050,000 | Moderate | ~3,150–3,650 sf Type V-B, CMU stem wall, wood frame, fully detailed MEP; $230–$290/sf range for rural North Florida commercial |
| Critical issue corrections (Issues #1–#7) | $100,000–$350,000 | Low–Moderate | Sprinkler, HVAC upsize, electrical, ADA, interface details, water service, permit corrections |
| **Total base case (corrected, as-permitted)** | **$950,000–$1,400,000** | Low–Moderate | Wide range reflects primarily the sprinkler and HVAC redesign uncertainty |

**ASSUMPTION:** No site civil costs (parking lot, utility service from main to building, exterior lighting, landscaping) are in the base case above because they are not designed in this set. I add these as a separate line in the recommended plan. **Confidence: Moderate that these are missing; Low on their cost range.**

---

## A. Cost-Side Value Engineering

### A-1. HVAC System Architecture — Multi-Zone Mini-Split vs. Single Large Packaged Unit
**What changes:** The corrected HVAC load is 12–16 tons (per confirmed Issue #1). The EOR's current approach (single-zone ducted split) scaled to that size would require a large rooftop or split unit with extensive ductwork across a 3,650 sf building with varied occupancy density. Alternative: **multi-zone ductless mini-split system** (e.g., Mitsubishi Electric, Daikin, or Carrier VRF-lite) with individual indoor cassettes in each major space (Bar/Lounge, Members Lounge, Fitness Room, Pro Shop, Offices) and a dedicated ventilation unit (ERV or DOAS) to handle the corrected OA requirement independently.

| Item | Base Case (corrected single-zone) | Mini-Split / DOAS Alternative | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equipment cost | $18,000–$28,000 (12–16-ton packaged) | $22,000–$35,000 (VRF-lite + DOAS) | +$4,000–+$7,000 |
| Ductwork | $15,000–$25,000 (extensive runs, 3,650 sf) | $4,000–$8,000 (minimal; linesets only) | -$11,000–-$17,000 |
| Electrical (panel, wire, breakers) | $6,000–$10,000 (one large circuit) | $8,000–$13,000 (multiple smaller circuits, lower MOCP per unit) | +$2,000–+$3,000 |
| Roof penetrations / structural | $3,000–$6,000 (single large curb) | $1,500–$3,000 (multiple small penetrations) | -$1,500–-$3,000 |
| **Net hard cost delta** | — | — | **-$6,500–-$10,000 savings** |

**Revenue/NOI delta:** Individual zone control allows the bar to run full cooling during evening events while the fitness room runs independently at a different setpoint during morning hours — real operating cost savings. Estimated $1,500–$3,500/year in reduced energy cost at Florida utility rates. **Directional; confidence: moderate.**

**Schedule effect:** Mini-split systems typically have shorter lead times than large packaged units; mini-split installation is also faster (no duct fabrication). Net schedule benefit: **1–2 weeks** in mechanical rough-in.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** The DOAS unit must be sized and specified by the MEP EOR as part of the required HVAC redesign (Issue #1). The A2L refrigerant transition (Issue #22) is actually easier with modern mini-split equipment, which is already transitioning to R-32/R-454B.

**Recommendation: ACCEPT.** Net savings $6,500–$10,000 hard cost plus ongoing energy savings. Should be incorporated into the mandatory HVAC redesign. **Confidence: Moderate.**

---

### A-2. Fire Sprinkler System Design — NFPA 13 vs. NFPA 13R
**What changes:** Issue #2 confirms a wet-pipe sprinkler system is required. The base case estimate uses NFPA 13 (full commercial standard). Alternative: **NFPA 13R** (residential/light commercial standard, permitted for buildings up to 4 stories with certain occupancy conditions). However, Group A-2 (bar) occupancies are **explicitly excluded from NFPA 13R** per its scope. Therefore this alternative applies only if the architect successfully separates the A-2 Bar/Lounge from the rest of the building with a fire-rated assembly, making the remainder (A-3 + M + B + S) potentially 13R-eligible.

| Item | NFPA 13 Full | NFPA 13R (if A-2 separated) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sprinkler heads | Full coverage every space including closets | Dwelling-unit-style coverage, fewer heads in non-sleeping areas | -15–25% head count |
| System cost | $45,000–$90,000 | $32,000–$60,000 | -$13,000–-$30,000 |
| Fire-rated separation cost | $0 | $8,000–$20,000 (1-hr rated wall, doors, fire dampers) | +$8,000–+$20,000 |
| **Net delta** | — | — | **-$5,000–-$10,000** |

**Reality check:** The Bar/Lounge and Members Lounge are designed as a connected open floor plan with no fire separation. Adding a rated wall changes the building program significantly and requires architectural and structural revisions. The NOI impact of walling off the bar from the lounge may be negative (reduced event flexibility). **NFPA 13R path is marginal at best and requires a material program change.**

**Recommendation: REJECT for 13R.** Accept the NFPA 13 cost and design the best open-plan bar/lounge the program allows. The $5,000–$10,000 potential savings do not justify the program disruption, the added fire-rated construction cost, and the design revision effort. **Confidence: High on rejection rationale.**

---

### A-3. Foundation — Reduce Footing Size If Geotechnical Report Supports Higher Bearing Value
**What changes:** The current 16"×36" perimeter footing is designed on an unresolved 1,500–2,000 psf bearing assumption. If the geotechnical report (required per Issue #4) returns a value of 2,500 psf or higher (common in North Florida upland sandy soils with competent bearing), the footing can potentially be reduced to a 12"×24" or 14"×30" configuration, saving concrete and excavation.

| Item | Base Case (16"×36") | Reduced (12"×24" at 2,500 psf) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Footing concrete (260 LF perimeter) | ~42 CY | ~18 CY | -24 CY |
| Concrete cost savings (@$175/CY placed) | — | — | -$4,200 |
| Excavation savings | — | — | -$800–-$1,500 |
| Rebar savings (minor) | — | — | -$500–-$1,000 |
| **Net delta** | — | — | **-$5,500–-$6,700** |

**Constraint:** Cannot be confirmed until geotechnical report is received. If the report returns 1,500 psf or lower, the footing must be upsized, not reduced — a cost increase. **This is a conditional VE item, not a guaranteed saving.**

**Recommendation: HOLD — evaluate after geotechnical report is received.** Do not redesign until data is in hand. Potential savings of $5,500–$6,700 are worth the EOR's 2-hour redesign time if the report supports it. **Confidence: Low on savings realization (depends on soils).**

---

### A-4. Covered Porch — Simplify Column and Portico Design
**What changes:** The front porch as designed has 6 square columns plus a projecting 2-column portico centered on the main entrance — a relatively elaborate architectural gesture. The portico (projecting beyond the porch roofline, requiring its own framing, roofing, and flashing) adds construction complexity and was identified as a source of coordination errors (column mislabel, two ceiling products, slab elevation conflict). Alternative: **eliminate the projecting portico and use a flat-fascia gable-end porch** with the same 6 columns, no projection. The porch retains its full width and depth; only the projecting center element is removed.

| Item | Base Case (with portico) | Simplified (flat porch) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Portico framing and roofing | $4,000–$7,000 | $0 | -$4,000–-$7,000 |
| Reduced coordination errors / RFI time | — | Eliminates Issues #13, #14 partially | -$1,000–$3,000 (saved RFI/redesign time) |
| Architectural fee for redesign | $0 (already designed) | $800–$1,500 (minor revision) | +$800–+$1,500 |
| **Net delta** | — | — | **-$4,200–-$8,500** |

**Revenue/NOI delta:** The portico is a curb-appeal element. Removing it slightly reduces the building's visual presence from the parking area, which could marginally affect first-impression quality for new members and resort guests. This is a real but unquantifiable negative. **Directional; confidence: low.**

**Plan amendment required:** Yes — architectural sheet revision required. Not an agency resubmittal if the footprint does not change (the porch outline stays the same); an architect's revision letter is sufficient.

**Recommendation: CONDITIONAL ACCEPT** — only if the owner agrees the portico is expendable. The savings are real but the curb-appeal cost is real too. Present to owner as an option, not a default. **Confidence: Moderate on savings.**

---

### A-5. Electrical — Correct Breaker Sizes as Part of HVAC Redesign (Zero-Cost VE)
**What changes:** Issues #1 and #3 together require both an HVAC redesign and a panel schedule revision. If the electrical EOR waits until the HVAC redesign is complete before issuing the corrected panel schedule, the panel is sized correctly the first time and the NEC violations are resolved without a separate revision cycle.

**Cost delta:** $0 additional cost vs. base; **saves $2,000–$8,000** in revision and potential rework cost vs. correcting the violations after the panel is set. This is pure sequencing discipline, not a design change.

**Recommendation: ACCEPT immediately.** Sequence the electrical revision after the HVAC redesign, not before. **Confidence: High.**

### A-6. Road Section, Site Pads, Electrical Pedestals, Stormwater — Menadier Civil Set
**Note:** These categories (road section, site pad type, pedestal spec, stormwater pond design, lift station) apply to the **Menadier Engineering civil set for the 215-site RV expansion**, which was reviewed separately. They do not apply to this 43-sheet building set. VE recommendations for those items belong in the Menadier civil VE analysis.

For this clubhouse project specifically, the only road/paving element is the **parking lot** (not yet designed — see Issue #20). When parking is designed, the following VE guidance applies:

- **Surface:** For an RV resort clubhouse parking area in rural North Florida, **chip seal over 6" compacted aggregate base** is approximately 35–45% cheaper than full-depth asphalt and is entirely appropriate for a low-traffic, low-speed parking application. ASSUMED unit cost: chip seal ~$2.50–$3.50/sy vs. asphalt ~$5.50–$7.50/sy.
- **Curb:** Eliminate curb and gutter; use grass swales for drainage (appropriate for North Florida sandy soils with good infiltration). Saves $12–$18/LF of curb.
- **ADA spaces:** Regardless of surface choice, ADA-designated spaces must be paved with a firm, stable surface — a small concrete or asphalt island for 2–3 ADA spaces within a chip-seal lot is code-compliant and cost-effective.

**Estimated savings vs. full-asphalt curbed lot (50 spaces, ~8,500 sy):** $18,000–$38,000. **Confidence: Moderate. ASSUMED 50 spaces and lot dimensions — parking design not yet complete.**

---

### A-7. Over-Specification Review — Plumbing Pipe Class and Concrete Strength
**What changes:** Two potential over-specifications are visible in the plan text:

1. **Concrete strength:** The structural notes specify 5,000 psi for walls and columns. For wood-frame Type V-B construction with CMU stem walls, 4,000 psi is the standard minimum per FBC and is adequate for this application. The 5,000 psi spec adds approximately 8–12% to the concrete material cost for those elements. **ASSUMED 15–20 CY of wall/column concrete affected.**
   - Savings: ~$400–$800. **Too small to pursue unless the structural EOR agrees without a redesign fee that exceeds the savings.**

2. **Water service pipe:** The MEP-required 1.5" service (or 2" with fire sprinklers) is appropriate and should not be reduced — it is already undersized relative to the fire protection requirement. **No savings available here without code compromise.**

**Recommendation on A-7:** The concrete over-specification saving ($400–$800) is below the EOR's minimum revision fee. **REJECT as a standalone VE item.** If the structural EOR is already revising the foundation design for another reason (geotechnical report result, footing depth correction), ask them to evaluate 4,000 psi walls at the same time — zero incremental cost.

---

## B. Revenue-Side Value-Add

> **Market input basis:** Golf Life Navigators 2025 report (8M+ data points, 55,000 buyers surveyed), cited in project brief. RV resort market rents estimated from 2024–2025 national averages for Class A/B resort properties in the Southeast US market. Treat all NOI deltas as **directional planning estimates**; a formal appraisal or feasibility study is needed for investment decisions.

---

### B-1. Bar/Lounge as a Revenue Center — Food & Beverage Programming
**What changes (no plan change required):** The Bar/Lounge (997 sf, 67 occupants, the largest room in the addition) is already designed as the primary revenue space. The Golf Life Navigators data confirms ~50% of buyers cite F&B quality as top-of-mind, with specific demand for a "sports bar" atmosphere and **breakfast service**. No plan change is needed; this is an operational programming recommendation.

| Revenue Stream | Estimated Annual Gross | Assumptions | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bar/beverage sales (resort guests + golf members, 91 existing + 215 expansion sites) | $120,000–$200,000/yr | 300 covered lives at buildout; $400–$670/site/year average F&B spend; 60–70% margin on beverage | Low–Moderate |
| Breakfast service (7 days, resort guests) | $40,000–$80,000/yr | 50 covers/day avg at $12–$15/cover, 250 operating days | Low |
| Golf 19th-hole F&B (existing 9-hole course) | $30,000–$60,000/yr | 30 rounds/day avg at $10–$15/round F&B attachment | Low |
| Private event rental (clubhouse buyout) | $15,000–$35,000/yr | 10–20 events/year at $1,500–$1,750/event | Low |
| **Total gross F&B revenue (stabilized)** | **$205,000–$375,000/yr** | — | Low |
| Less: F&B operating costs (food cost, labor, supplies) | ($140,000–$260,000/yr) | 65–70% operating cost ratio for small venue F&B | Low |
| **Net F&B contribution** | **$65,000–$115,000/yr** | — | Low |
| **Capitalized NOI delta (@8.5% cap rate)** | **$765,000–$1,350,000** | Directional only | Low |

**This is the single highest-return element of the entire addition.** The building cost is justified primarily by this revenue stream. **Directional; treat as a range, not a projection.**

**Plan change required:** No. Operational decision only. However, if a commercial kitchen (even a minimal prep kitchen with a hood system, 3-bay sink, and health department permit) is added behind the bar, F&B revenue potential roughly doubles. This IS a plan change — see B-2.

---

### B-2. Add a Minimal Commercial Prep Kitchen Behind the Bar
**What changes:** The Bar/Lounge as designed appears to be a service bar (no kitchen shown, no hood, no commercial cooking equipment). Adding a **Type II hood, 3-bay sink, undercounter refrigeration, and a flat-top grill/panini press** behind the bar — a "snack bar" or "pub kitchen" rather than a full restaurant kitchen — enables breakfast service, light lunch, and bar food without a full commercial kitchen permit. ASSUMED approximately 80–100 sf of bar back-of-house is available within the existing 997 sf Bar/Lounge footprint.

| Item | Cost Delta | Revenue Delta (annual) | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type II hood (vs. Type I — no cooking fires required for snack bar) | $8,000–$15,000 | — | Moderate |
| 3-bay sink, undercounter refrigeration, prep table | $6,000–$10,000 | — | Moderate |
| Plumbing for additional fixtures | $3,000–$6,000 | — | Moderate |
| Electrical for equipment | $2,000–$4,000 | — | Moderate |
| Health department plan review and permit | $1,500–$3,000 | — | Moderate |
| **Total incremental hard cost** | **$20,500–$38,000** | — | Moderate |
| Incremental annual gross F&B revenue enabled | — | $60,000–$120,000 | Low |
| Incremental NOI (@65% cost ratio) | — | $21,000–$42,000/yr | Low |
| **Capitalized NOI delta (@8.5% cap)** | — | **$247,000–$494,000** | Low |
| **Return on incremental capital** | — | **550–1,200%** | Low |

**Plan change required:** Yes — architectural, MEP (plumbing, mechanical/hood), and health department plan amendment required. **Agency resubmittal to Madison County building department and Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) Division of Hotels and Restaurants for food service license.**

**Recommendation: STRONG ACCEPT.** Even at conservative estimates, this is the highest-return incremental investment available on this project. The Golf Life Navigators data (50% of buyers cite F&B quality, specific demand for breakfast) independently validates the demand. **Confidence: Moderate on cost delta; Low on revenue (market-dependent).**

---

### B-3. Poolside Food & Beverage Service Connection
**What changes:** The existing pool at the resort is not part of this addition, but the Golf Life Navigators data explicitly validates that 55% of buyers want **poolside F&B service** and 44% of buyers cite the pool as a valued amenity. A **walk-up service window or pass-through from the Bar/Lounge to an exterior poolside area** would capture this demand.

ASSUMED: the pool is within reasonable proximity to the south face of the clubhouse addition (not confirmed from the 43-sheet set — pool location not shown). If the pool is within 50–100 feet of the covered porch, a walk-up window cut into the south wall of the Bar/Lounge (or serving from the porch) is architecturally and structurally feasible.

| Item | Cost Delta | Revenue Delta | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Walk-up service window (CMU wall penetration, counter, shutter) | $4,000–$9,000 | — | Low |
| Extended porch or path to pool area (not in current scope) | $5,000–$15,000 | — | Low |
| **Total incremental cost** | **$9,000–$24,000** | — | Low |
| Incremental poolside F&B revenue (seasonal, North Florida) | — | $15,000–$40,000/yr | Low |
| Incremental NOI (@65% cost ratio) | — | $5,250–$14,000/yr | Low |
| **Capitalized NOI delta (@8.5% cap)** | — | **$62,000–$165,000** | Low |

**Plan change required:** Yes — architectural sheet revision, structural EOR approval of wall penetration, MEP for the service window. Agency resubmittal likely if the exterior footprint changes.

**Constraint:** Pool proximity must be confirmed before this is designed. If the pool is more than 150 feet from the bar, the operating model changes (food delivery logistics).

**Recommendation: ACCEPT if pool proximity is confirmed.** Low cost, meaningful revenue upside, and directly validated by market data. **Confidence: Low overall (pool location unknown from this set).**

---

### B-4. Fitness Room — Premium Equipment Package and Membership Upsell
**What changes (no plan change required):** The Fitness Room (361 sf, A-3) is designed as a room; no equipment is specified in this set. The Golf Life Navigators data confirms a **6% year-over-year increase in health/wellness demand** with specific demand for modern cardio equipment. A premium equipment package (4–6 pieces of commercial-grade cardio equipment plus free weights and a mirror wall) transforms a bare room into a genuine amenity that supports a membership tier upsell.

| Item | Cost Delta (one-time) | Revenue Delta | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commercial cardio equipment (4–6 units, Precor/Life Fitness) | $20,000–$40,000 | — | Moderate |
| Free weight station + mirrors | $3,000–$6,000 | — | Moderate |
| Equipment maintenance contract | $1,500–$3,000/yr | — | Moderate |
| **Total incremental cost** | **$23,000–$46,000** | — | Moderate |
| Premium "resort member" tier vs. standard tier (50 members at $20–$40/month premium) | — | $12,000–$24,000/yr | Low |
| Reduced member churn (retention value) | — | $5,000–$15,000/yr (avoided re-leasing cost) | Low |
| **Net NOI delta** | — | **$13,500–$36,000/yr** | Low |
| **Capitalized NOI delta (@8.5% cap)** | — | **$159,000–$424,000** | Low |
| **Return on incremental capital** | — | **350–780%** | Low |

**Plan change required:** No (equipment purchase only; no structural or MEP change needed for standard commercial cardio equipment within a 361 sf room with 11' ceilings and existing electrical service). Confirm with MEP EOR that dedicated 20A circuits are available for each cardio unit.

**Recommendation: ACCEPT.** High return, no plan change required, directly validated by market data. **Confidence: Moderate on cost; Low on revenue.**

---

### B-5. Pro Shop Revenue Optimization — Golf + Resort Retail
**What changes (minor plan change):** The Pro Shop (247 sf, M occupancy) is appropriately sized for a 9-hole course operation. Revenue optimization does not require a plan change but a **retail display and POS system investment** (approximately $8,000–$15,000) transforms it from a storage-adjacent space into a genuine retail revenue center. For the 215-site expansion adding 215 households as potential customers, the pro shop has a natural expanded market.

| Revenue Stream | Annual Estimate | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Golf equipment/apparel retail | $15,000–$30,000/yr | Low |
| Green fees and cart rental (existing course) | $40,000–$80,000/yr (existing, not incremental) | Low |
| Resort-branded merchandise | $5,000–$12,000/yr | Low |
| **Incremental NOI from retail investment** | **$8,000–$20,000/yr** | Low |

**Recommendation: ACCEPT as a low-cost operational decision.** No plan change required. **Confidence: Low on revenue.**

---

### B-6. Members Lounge — Private Event and Pickleball Tournament Hub
**What changes:** The existing pickleball courts (referenced in project brief as a strong member-retention driver per Golf Life Navigators data) and the Members Lounge (805 sf, A-3, 54 occupants) create a natural combination: **pickleball tournament hosting with post-match social events in the Members Lounge.** This requires no plan change but does require operational programming and potentially a small equipment storage area (folding tables, portable bar cart). The large Storage room (319 sf) adjacent to the Members Lounge is well-positioned for this purpose.

**NOI delta (directional):** 6–10 hosted events/year at $500–$1,200 net per event = **$3,000–$12,000/yr incremental.** Small but zero capital cost.

**Recommendation: ACCEPT as an operational decision.** No plan change, no capital cost. **Confidence: Low on revenue.**

---

### B-7. Submetering and Utility Pass-Through
**What changes:** This clubhouse addition does not have individual site utility metering (it is a single building, not a multi-tenant site). However, the **broader resort operation** (existing 91 sites + 215-site expansion) benefits enormously from individual site water and electric submetering. This is a recommendation for the Menadier civil set, not this building set.

For this building specifically: if the building hosts **member or tenant uses** (e.g., a pro shop operator or F&B concessionaire), a **submeter for the commercial kitchen circuit and the bar's refrigeration circuits** allows utility cost pass-through to the concessionaire. Cost: $1,500–$3,000 for 2–3 submeters. Revenue: direct utility cost recovery from concessionaire, estimated $3,000–$6,000/yr depending on kitchen load.

**Plan change required:** Minor MEP revision to add submeter locations on the panel schedule. **No agency resubmittal required** if submeters are on the load side of the main meter (within the building's own electrical system).

**Recommendation: ACCEPT as part of the mandatory electrical panel redesign (Issue #3).** Negligible incremental cost; meaningful long-term cost recovery. **Confidence: Moderate.**

---

## C. Phasing and Capital Alternatives

### C-1. Minimum Viable Phase 1 — Open and Cash-Flow
**Current plan:** The addition is designed as a single-phase project — all rooms built simultaneously. Given the seven confirmed critical issues (particularly sprinkler, HVAC, and ADA corrections), the project cannot be occupied until all critical issues are resolved. There is no phasing shown in the 43-sheet set.

**Alternative Phase 1 (minimum openable):** Build the following rooms first, deferring the balance:

| Space | Area | Priority | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bar/Lounge | 997 sf | Phase 1 — highest revenue | Largest NOI generator |
| Members Lounge | 805 sf | Phase 1 — core amenity | Member retention |
| Both restrooms | 237 sf | Phase 1 — required for occupancy | Code requirement |
| Mechanical room | 43 sf | Phase 1 — required | HVAC service |
| Covered porch | 490 sf | Phase 1 — curb appeal | Guest first impression |
| **Phase 1 subtotal** | **~2,572 sf** | — | ~70% of new building area |

| Space | Area | Priority | Reason for Deferral |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fitness Room | 361 sf | Phase 2 | Equipment lead time; not required for occupancy |
| Pro Shop | 247 sf | Phase 2 | Revenue positive but not day-one critical |
| Office | 97 sf | Phase 2 | Administrative function; can use temporary space |
| Large Storage | 319 sf | Phase 2 | Deferred without operational impact |

**Phase 1 hard cost estimate:** ~$620,000–$820,000 (proportional to area, with sprinkler and HVAC corrections carried entirely in Phase 1 since the systems serve the whole building). **Confidence: Low — phasing does not proportionally reduce infrastructure costs.**

**Critical constraint:** The sprinkler system, HVAC system, and fire service must be sized for the **full building** even in Phase 1, because the Phase 2 spaces will be connected. Phasing this building does not provide meaningful infrastructure cost savings — it only defers the interior fit-out of the smaller rooms. **The capital savings from phasing are limited to approximately $80,000–$130,000 (Phase 2 interior construction only), while the schedule benefit is 3–6 weeks.**

**Recommendation: PARTIAL ACCEPT on phasing.** Build Phase 1 as the Bar/Lounge + Members Lounge + restrooms + porch, with all infrastructure (sprinkler, HVAC, electrical) sized for the full building. Defer Fitness Room fit-out and equipment, Pro Shop millwork, and large Storage shelving to Phase 2 after the building is generating revenue. This is a **finish deferral, not a structural phasing** — the framing and MEP rough-in for the full building should be completed in one mobilization to avoid re-mobilization costs. **Confidence: Moderate.**

---

### C-2. Developer-Owned Utilities — Asset vs. Liability Analysis
**Wastewater:** If the existing drainfield is inadequate for 140-occupant clubhouse + 215-site expansion (a real possibility per Issue #19), the developer faces a choice between:

| Option | Capital Cost | Operating Cost | Asset Value | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Municipal sewer connection (if available) | $50,000–$200,000 (tap fee + line extension) | $800–$2,000/month utility bill | Zero — it's an expense | Preferred if available; clean, no regulatory liability |
| Package WWTP (developer-owned) | $150,000–$400,000 installed | $15,000–$40,000/yr O&M + permit | Real asset; can be expanded; potentially sellable to utility | Consider if municipal sewer unavailable or very expensive |
| Drainfield expansion (if soils permit) | $20,000–$80,000 | Minimal | No asset value; regulatory liability | Cheapest if soils support it; get FDOH confirmation |
| Gravity sewer to municipal (long extension) | $200,000–$600,000+ (distance-dependent) | $800–$2,000/month | Zero | Only if extension distance is short |

**ASSUMPTION:** Municipal sewer availability at this address in Madison County is unknown from the drawings. Madison is a small county seat; sewer availability at a rural golf course/RV property 445 Country Club Rd is uncertain. **Owner must confirm with Madison County Utility Department before wastewater design proceeds.**

**Developer-owned well (water supply):** The existing water source appears to be a municipal connection (3" main in the Menadier civil set). A developer-owned well is theoretically possible but would require FDEP permitting, fire flow testing, and water treatment — generally not cost-competitive with municipal connection for a property this size unless the utility refuses to upsize the service.

**Recommendation on utilities:** Pursue municipal connections for both water and sewer if available. If wastewater requires a package plant, treat it as infrastructure (not an asset to monetize) and size it for the full 215-site + clubhouse load to avoid a second plant installation.

---

### C-3. Structural Choices That Foreclose Future Expansion
**Issue:** This addition is drawn hard against the existing building with no interface details (Issue #5). Beyond the immediate safety and code problems, this placement creates a future constraint: **the new building's south face (covered porch) and north face (existing building) both limit future horizontal expansion.** The only unobstructed expansion direction is east or west along the building's long axis.

**Optionality-preserving actions:**

| Action | Cost Now | Cost to Preserve Option | Value of Option |
|---|---|---|---|
| Design the east gable end with a removable (non-load-bearing) wall section for future eastward expansion | $500–$1,500 (framing modification) | $500–$1,500 | Eliminates $8,000–$20,000 future demo and reframing cost | 
| Upsize the main electrical panel to 400A (vs. minimum required for current load) | $1,500–$3,000 incremental | $1,500–$3,000 | Avoids $5,000–$12,000 panel replacement if future expansion adds load |
| Install a capped 2" sanitary stub-out on the east wall for future restroom addition | $800–$1,500 | $800–$1,500 | Avoids $4,000–$8,000 of concrete saw-cutting if restrooms must expand |
| Size the sprinkler system main (when designed) for 25% additional capacity | $1,000–$2,500 incremental in pipe sizing | $1,000–$2,500 | Avoids $6,000–$15,000 of fire line rework if building expands |

**Total cost to preserve expansion optionality: $3,800–$8,500.** This is one of the highest-return investments on the project — optionality is cheap at rough-in and expensive after close-in. **Confidence: High on cost; Moderate on future value.**

**Recommendation: ACCEPT all four optionality-preservation actions.** Incorporate into the mandatory engineering revisions already required by the critical issues. **These should be added to the RFI list for each respective EOR.**

---

### C-4. Road Dead-Ends and Utility Mains — Menadier Civil Set
These items apply to the Menadier civil set (215-site RV expansion), not to this building set. The one relevant cross-project note: the water main serving this clubhouse building should be **looped back to the RV expansion's distribution system** (not dead-ended at the building) to provide flushing capability and redundant supply — particularly important if fire sprinklers are added. This should be a coordination requirement in the joint RFI between the two design teams (Issue #6).

---

## Recommended Alternative Plan — Top 5 Changes

### Summary Table

| Change | Hard Cost Delta | Soft Cost Delta | Annual NOI Delta | Cap Value Delta (@8.5%) | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Add minimal commercial prep kitchen behind bar (B-2) | +$20,500–+$38,000 | +$3,000–$5,000 | +$21,000–$42,000 | +$247,000–+$494,000 | Low–Moderate |

| 5. Chip-seal parking lot instead of full-asphalt (A-6, when parking is designed) | -$18,000–-$38,000 | $0 | $0 | $0 | Moderate |
| **Net of top 5** | **+$22,800–+$44,500 net increase** | **+$3,000–$5,000** | **+$36,000–$81,500/yr** | **+$454,000–+$1,015,000** | Low |

### Revised Cost and Program (Recommended Plan)

| Building construction (hard) | $950,000–$1,400,000 | $975,000–$1,445,000 | +$25,000 (kitchen and optionality additions net of HVAC savings) |

| **Capitalized value of building (@8.5% cap)** | **$765,000–$1,350,000** | **$1,188,000–$2,312,000** | **+$423,000–+$962,000** |

---

> **Critical framing note for the reader:** The approved 43-sheet set is a **building-only construction document** for the clubhouse addition. It is not a civil site plan for an RV park expansion. Accordingly, "approved envelope" for this analysis means: the interior and exterior of the new ~3,150–3,650 sf clubhouse addition, the ~490 sf covered front porch, the immediate building perimeter (landscaping, signage, lighting within the building's approved footprint zone), and the existing resort amenities (pool, golf course, pickleball courts, fitness room) that are referenced in the program but not altered by this permit. ### Most Cost-Effective Amenity: **Bar/Lounge F&B Programming (Rank #1)**

The Bar/Lounge F&B program beats every other idea on this specific site because:
1. **The approved plans already gave it the infrastructure**: the 998 sf Bar/Lounge (the largest room in the addition, A-2 occupancy, 67 seats) is designed and permitted exactly for this use. No footprint change, no structural change.
2. **The demand evidence is exceptional**: Golf Life Navigators 2025 (8M+ data points, 55,000 buyers surveyed) explicitly identifies F&B quality and sports-bar atmosphere as top-of-mind for ~50% of buyers at this exact asset type — not a generic hospitality finding, but one specific to golf-and-RV resort guests.
3. **The payback is sub-1-year**: at $25,000–$32,000 installed cost and ~$45,000 net NOI contribution, this is a less-than-1-year payback even at conservative revenue assumptions.
4. **It has the highest synergy multiplier**: every other revenue idea (poolside service, golf tournaments, membership program, porch events) drives incremental F&B revenue that flows back through this same Bar/Lounge. It is the hub of the revenue network.

## Excluded — Would Require Plan Amendment

The following ideas were considered and excluded because they would change something the site plan or civil approval was issued on, require an amendment to the approved building footprint, alter utility routing/sizing, or change an approved condition. They are listed here so the owner knows what was left on the table:

1. **Adding a kitchen hood and grease trap for a full-service restaurant** — would require a new exhaust penetration through the approved roof, a grease trap added to the approved plumbing/site utility plan, and a change in occupancy classification from A-2 to A-2 + B (food service) — all requiring plan amendment and health department permit.
2. **Adding an outdoor tiki bar or poolside bar structure** — any new structure adjacent to the pool would constitute a new building footprint not shown on the approved site plan.
3. **Adding EV charging stations to the parking area** — the parking area is not designed in this building permit set; EV chargers require a civil/electrical amendment to the site plan and potentially to the utility service sizing.
4. **Adding a dog park fence on resort open space** — fencing not shown on the approved site plan is a site plan amendment in most Florida jurisdictions.
5. **Adding a golf cart path or paved trail connecting the clubhouse to the golf course or RV sites** — any new paved surface changes the approved impervious area and stormwater design.
6. **Expanding the covered porch depth or adding a screened enclosure** — any change to the approved building footprint or porch dimensions requires a building permit amendment.
7. **Adding a propane tank for a future outdoor fireplace or grill** — propane tank placement and routing would need to be shown on the approved site plan and mechanical plan; this is a separate permit that may also require site plan amendment depending on tank size and setback.
8. **Adding a solar PV array on the approved roof** — changes the approved roof loading (structural amendment required) and may require a utility interconnection agreement not currently in the approved set.
9. **Upsizing the water service or adding a separate fire line** — this is a **required correction** (Critical Issue #2 and #6), not a value-engineering idea; it requires a utility permit and civil plan amendment, and is already flagged in the Error Register.

cross_run_notes: This is a SEPARATE project from the Madison RV park expansion (215-site RV plan set, a different engineer -- Menadier Engineering vs. this addition's Hammond Design Group). They share a property and a few utility questions but are two distinct construction document sets.

This review's 103-item register was built by 5 parallel specialist visual reviews (Opus), each reading every sheet image directly at full resolution -- the plan set's own PDF text layer is sparse (Archicad export, mostly title-block boilerplate) so a text-only AI pass would have missed nearly everything. Every finding cites the specific sheet(s) it came from.

THE SINGLE MOST ACTIONABLE FINDING: the HVAC design is built on a ventilation calculation that modeled only 27 of the real 140 building occupants at 0.00 CFM/person -- correcting it (as code requires) pushes the realistic cooling load from the ~6-ton system currently specified to an estimated 12-16 tons. Two electrical breakers on the existing (undersized) HVAC equipment also exceed their own nameplate maximum overcurrent rating -- a real NEC violation independent of the sizing question.

A real, confirmed coordination failure with the separate RV park expansion project: this clubhouse's own MEP engineer requires a 1.5" water service, but the RV park's civil engineer (a different firm, never in contact with this one) is only bringing a 1" line to this same building. Get the two engineers talking before either utility scope is built.

Multiple real, currently-cheap-to-fix ADA violations: the main entrance and two other double doors fail clear-width requirements (equal-leaf pairs netting under 32" clear), and no panic hardware is specified on exit doors serving the 67-occupant bar or 54-occupant lounge (both over the 50-occupant threshold requiring it).

big_picture_md:
## 1. What will this cost?

The single independent estimate puts this project at **$2.36 million total** (range $1.65M–$3.54M at AACE Class 4 accuracy). That range is wide for one reason above all others: there's a $488K parking-lot allowance in the number because no parking layout exists in the plan set — if adequate parking is already on-site, the realistic range drops to roughly $1.3M–$1.9M. Confirm that first, because it's the biggest single swing in the whole budget. Hard construction before contingency and soft costs is $1.6M; the 25% contingency (higher than normal) reflects three unresolved unknowns — no geotech report, no sprinkler design, and an uncertain wastewater situation that could run anywhere from $25K to $200K+.

---

## 2. What can we do to reduce it?

**The best-supported single move is confirming whether the parking lot already exists** — that one answer removes up to $452K from the budget with zero design effort. Beyond that, specify chip-seal over compacted aggregate base instead of full-depth asphalt when the parking is eventually designed; that saves $18K–$38K on its own and is entirely appropriate for low-speed RV resort use. Second-best: when the HVAC is redesigned (which is mandatory — see below), specify a multi-zone ductless mini-split plus a dedicated outdoor-air unit instead of one large ducted system. That approach saves $6,500–$10,000 in hard cost by eliminating most of the ductwork runs, and then saves another $1,500–$3,500 per year in energy.

---

## 3. What else would you recommend?

**Stop the clock on equipment orders and underground utility work until two things are resolved.** First, the building almost certainly needs a full wet-pipe sprinkler system that nobody has designed — the bar and lounge together push past the occupant-load threshold that triggers it under Florida code, and if it's caught mid-construction rather than now, it forces a redesign of the coffered ceilings, the water service size, and potentially the roof. Get a fire-protection engineer on the phone this week. Second, the HVAC engineer modeled only 27 of the real 140 occupants and specified a 6-ton unit for a load that's realistically 12–16 tons — do not order that equipment. Separately, the MEP engineer is calling for a 1.5-inch water service to this building while the RV park's civil engineer is running only a 1-inch line to the same building — those two have never compared notes, and if the 1-inch line gets buried first it will need to be torn out and replaced. One phone call between those two engineers before any dirt moves solves that entirely.

Resolve the water-service size conflict with the separate RV park expansion's civil engineer (1.5" needed here vs. 1" being designed)

Here is my independent review of the Madison Country Club Addition plan set, evaluated strictly through the lens of a permanent owner-operator holding the asset for 40–50 years.

## 1. What will this cost?

**Estimated Vertical Construction Cost:** $950,000 – $1,250,000 (ASSUMED $300 – $400 per square foot)
**Site/Civil/Earthwork & Utility Laterals:** UNKNOWN (cannot be reliably estimated from the text provided)

**Reasoning:**
*   **Building Size:** The total conditioned/covered footprint is OBSERVED to be ~3,150 SF (Sheet Index notes 3,149.95 ft² across 10 rooms, though the Cover Sheet also lists an overall alteration square footage of 2,909.98 SF). I have ASSUMED the ~3,150 SF figure for estimating.
*   **Quality & Finishes:** This is a commercial clubhouse/assembly space with high-end, long-lasting exterior finishes (OBSERVED: James Hardie board-and-batten, brick cladding, and standing seam metal roof on Sheet A1.03) and custom interior finishes (OBSERVED: wood coffered ceilings, electric fireplace, and commercial bar equipment on Sheets A1.03 and A5.01). 
*   **Demolition:** The plans call for the total demolition of the existing roof, slab, and foundation in the affected zone (OBSERVED on AD1.01). 
*   **Florida Market:** Given the Tallahassee/Madison, FL market, Type V-B wood-framed commercial assembly buildings with high-end architectural finishes and commercial bar tie-ins currently trade in the $300–$400/SF range for vertical construction alone. 

## 2. What can we do to reduce it?

As a 50-year hold, we must reject any "value engineering" that saves pennies today but costs dollars in future maintenance. Here are concrete adjustments to the plans to optimize long-term ownership costs:

*   **Upgrade Slab Reinforcement (Reject WWF):** The foundation plan specifies "6x6 - W2.9xW2.9 WWF" (Welded Wire Fabric) for the 4" slab on grade (OBSERVED on S-1.1 and S-2.1). *40-Year View:* WWF is notoriously difficult to install correctly; it almost always ends up trampled to the bottom of the slab where it provides zero crack-control benefit. Over 40 years, this leads to slab cracking, moisture intrusion, and failed floor finishes. *Action:* Replace WWF with macro-synthetic fibers or #3 rebar at 18" O.C. It will cost marginally more upfront but will save tens of thousands in future flooring remediation.
*   **Upgrade the Vapor Barrier:** The structural notes call for a standard "6 MIL POLYETHYLENE SHEETING" under the interior slabs (OBSERVED on S-0.1). *40-Year View:* 6-mil poly is easily punctured by workers' boots and rebar chairs during the pour. In Florida's humid climate, slab moisture vapor transmission is a leading cause of flooring failure. *Action:* Upgrade to a minimum 10-mil or 15-mil puncture-resistant vapor retarder (e.g., Stego Wrap).
*   **Eliminate "Flex Duct" for Main HVAC Runs:** The mechanical legend indicates "6" FLEX DUCT U.N.O." (OBSERVED on M1.01). *40-Year View:* Flexible ductwork sags over time, collects dust, is easily crushed in the attic, and degrades, leading to severely restricted airflow, higher energy bills, and premature HVAC compressor failure. *Action:* Mandate rigid sheet metal for all trunk lines, allowing flex duct *only* for the final 3-to-5-foot runouts to individual ceiling diffusers.
*   **Rethink or Isolate the Roof Cupola:** The exterior elevations and sections feature a "Prefabricated Decorative Cupola" on a standing seam metal roof (OBSERVED on A3.01 and S-2.6). *40-Year View:* Standing seam roofs are fantastic for a 50-year hold, but roof penetrations are the enemy of longevity. A heavy cupola creates complex flashing requirements and acts as a long-term leak risk. *Action:* If the cupola is required for aesthetic reasons, ensure it is completely "surface mounted" (purely decorative) with zero penetration through the actual roof decking/underlayment, or delete it entirely to preserve the metal roof's pristine envelope.
*   **Evaluate CMU vs. Wood Framing for Exterior Walls:** The plans call for 2x6 exterior wood framing on top of CMU stem walls (OBSERVED on S-1.2). *40-Year View:* In a humid, termite-prone Florida environment, wood framing at grade level is a liability. *Action:* Since the mason is already mobilized to build CMU stem walls, price the delta to run CMU all the way up to the roof tie-beam for the exterior shell. It may cost slightly more today, but it offers superior hurricane resistance, zero termite risk, and drastically lower insurance premiums over a 50-year hold.

## 3. What else would you recommend?

*   **Major Risk - No Geotech Report:** The structural notes state: "NO GEO-TECHNICAL REPORT HAS BEEN PROVIDED. ALLOWABLE SOIL BEARING PRESSURES ARE ASSUMED..." (OBSERVED on S-0.1). *Action:* **Do not break ground without a soil boring.** Assuming a 2,000 PSF bearing capacity is a massive financial risk; if you hit unsuitable soils or organic material during foundation excavation, you will face catastrophic change orders.
*   **Structural Note Conflict:** On sheet S-0.1 under "Shallow Foundations", Note 2 appears twice with conflicting information. The first says footing sizes are based on "2000 PSF", and the very next note says they are based on "1500 PSF" (OBSERVED). *Action:* Issue an RFI to the Structural Engineer of Record to clarify the actual design assumption before submitting for permit.
*   **Bar Equipment Exhaust/Ventilation:** The bar equipment plan includes a "Countertop Pizza Oven" and a "Hot Dog Roller" (OBSERVED on A5.01). *Action:* Verify with the local fire marshal and health department if this specific pizza oven requires a Type I or Type II commercial exhaust hood. The mechanical notes currently do not explicitly show commercial kitchen exhaust systems. Adding a commercial hood retrospectively is wildly expensive.
*   **ADA Thresholds vs. Water Intrusion:** Detail 6 on A7.01 details a "1/2" MAX THRESHOLD" for ADA compliance at exterior doors. *Action:* Because there is no step-down, wind-driven rain can easily breach a 1/2" threshold. Ensure the civil plans include a generous outward slope (min 2%) on the exterior porch/walkways immediately leading away from these doors, and specify a commercial threshold with a built-in pan flashing or trench drain to protect the interior lounge flooring.

## Confidence notes
*   **Site/Civil & Earthwork:** UNKNOWN. No civil plans, grading, or landscape drawings were provided in the text. I cannot reliably estimate earthwork cut/fill, paving, or stormwater management costs.
*   **Utilities:** UNKNOWN. While the demo plan mentions "disconnect and seal any utilities", the size and length of the *new* domestic water, sanitary sewer, and electrical laterals required to service this expanded 3,150 SF building cannot be reliably estimated from the text provided.
*   **FF&E (Furniture, Fixtures, & Equipment):** UNKNOWN. Televisions, loose furniture, locker room fit-outs, and specific POS systems are noted as "By Owner" or "Not in Contract" and are excluded from my cost envelope.
